newsitem.title: USA: CalEnergy launches bid for N.Y. utility.
newsitem.headline: CalEnergy launches bid for N.Y. utility.

text.p: Power company CalEnergy Co. Inc. said on Tuesday it would launch a hostile $159 million bid for 9.9 percent of New York State Electric & Gas Corp. in the first step of an effort to buy the whole utility.

The Omaha, Neb.-based independent power producer offered to buy the stake for $24.50 per share in cash and said it would be willing to raise the offer to $27.50 per share for all of the stock if NYSEG agreed to a friendly deal.
The higher offer would be worth $1.9 billion based on NYSEG's 69.4 million outstanding shares. NYSEG also has $1.6 billion in debt.

If successful, the transaction would propel power producer CalEnergy into the electricity distribution business in the Northeast in the latest in a long list of transactions to hit the once-sleepy utility industry, which is now in the throes of deregulation.

"Our strong preference would be to work together with you and the NYSEG board to complete a negotiated transaction," CalEnergy Chairman David Sokol wrote in a letter to NYSEG Chairman Wesley con Schack.

But Sokol also said that CalEnergy was prepared to launch an aggressive attack on Binghamton, N.Y.-based NYSEG and would pursue a proxy fight or take other actions if necessary. He said CalEnergy has $2 billion in financing committed for the deal.
CalEnergy has a solid track record of acquisitions and last year completed a rare hostile takeover in the industry, buying British utility Northern Electric Plc. for $1.3 billion.
"We at CalEnergy finish what we start," Sokol told analysts in a telephone conference call.
New York State Electric's stock jumped $3.125 to $24.50 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange. CalEnergy fell $1.8125 to $38.75, also on the NYSE.
NYSEG said it would review the offer and urged sharheolders to take no action until its board issued a recommendation on the bid.

CalEnergy said it was launching the hostile bid after NYSEG decided not to pursue a friendly transaction. Sokol said he held talks with von Schack on July 10, and was surprised to be notified on July 12 that the company's board had determined a transaction was not a priority and could not be conducted on a timely basis.

Although NYSEG does not have a poison pill anti-takeover plan in place to deter a transaction, Sokol said the 9.9 percent stake was the largest amount that could be acquired without certain regulatory approvals. He also said CalEnergy already owns about 240,000 shares of NYSEG.

The bid surprised Wall Street, where analysts and investors questioned the logic of launching a hostile bid for a high-cost, low-growth utility that operates in a market wracked by uncertainty. They said NYSEG, which is battling regulators over rates, is far less attractive than other utilities that also could provide CalEnergy with a foothold in the Northeast electricity distribution business.
NYSEG "is a very ordinary utility. It's not one of the ones that are better-situated," said Barry Abramson of PaineWebber Inc.
Sokol defended CalEnergy's choice of a target, saying an acquisition would make NYSEG an aggressive competitor in an industry grapplying with deregulation.

"You've got a historically regulated monopoly business that's moving toward competition. We're very comfortable understanding what those challenges are to them and we think, solving them and in fact, growing the business and going forward in a competitive way," he told analysts.

Unlike many of the transactions taking hold of corporate America, Sokol said the acquisition of NYSEG is not about consolidation and cost-cutting. The proposed deal calls for CalEnergy to maintain NYSEG as a separate operating business and keep its existing corporate headquarters.
CalEnergy declined to discuss the potential deal's impact on earnings, saying only that its transactions historically have been accretive.

"It seems to me an awful lot of utility mergers are ... people walking two by two onto Noah's ark just trying to avoid the flood. We think the transaction to an independent marketplace is much more than just deciding whose furniture should be kept and whose furniture should be gotten rid of," Sokol said.

But analysts were uncomfortable with that explanation and expressed scepticism over Sokol's estimate that a deal could be completed in nine to 12 months. Utility transactions are typically slow to receive regulatory approvals.
"For the life of me, I don't know why they picked NYSEG," said Ed Tirello of NatWest Securities Corp.
The tender offer, which would be conducted by CalEnergy subsidiary CE Electric Inc., calls for shareholders tendering their shares to retain the 35-cent dividend payable in August.
